list.listitem: Suspect severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) in infants presenting with severe respiratory infections, persistent oral thrush, persistent diarrhea, failure to thrive, and age-related lymphopenia. C

Refer suspected cases to an immunologist or specialist center for further clinical and laboratory evaluation and genetic testing. These are required to establish the diagnosis, determine the specific underlying genetic abnormality, and commence appropriate treatment. B

SCID is treatable by allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation, enzyme replacement therapy (for some forms of SCID), and gene therapy (for some forms). Early identification and immediate referral to specialist centers provides the best chance for optimal survival. B

background.definition: Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) describes a heterogeneous group of monogenic disorders that cause profound deficiency of T cells (+/- B cells) with consequent severe impairment of cellular and humoral immunity. If untreated, SCID has 100% mortality by the age of 2 years. Most cases in the USA are identified through newborn screening with the T-cell receptor excision circles (TREC) quantification test.

list.listitem: The incidence of SCID in the USA has been estimated at 1:58,000 live births (95% CI, 1:46,000 – 1:80,000).

The incidence of SCID is higher in the Navajo Nation in the southwestern USA where it is estimated at 1:1580 – 1:2000 due to the presence of a founder truncation mutation in a single gene. (DCLRE1C gene, aka Artemis gene).
California began screening newborns for SCID in 2010. During a 6.5 year period with 3.25 million births, 50 cases of SCID were identified (a rate of 1 in 65,000 live births).
Inherited or de novo monogenic defects that affect normal T-cell development and function, and B cell ability to form specific antibodies.

More than 20 genetic defects have been described that result SCID. A study of newborn screening in 11 states showed that male infants were predominantly affected and X-linked SCID accounted for 19% of cases.

Mutations in heterogenous genes cause developmental blocks at different points in T-lymphocyte differentiation, resulting in low T-cell numbers and T-cell dysfunction. In the absence of T-cell help to B cells, there are defective antibody responses causing combined cellular and antibody immunodeficiency.
In some forms of SCID (eg T-B- form), B cell differentiation is directly affected, causing low B cell numbers. Other cell lines may also be affected.

Mutations causing complete absence of affected genes cause “typical SCIDs” with early onset of symptoms, while hypomorphic mutations causing partial function of affected genes manifest as “atypical (or leaky) SCIDs”, which present later in childhood.

SCID patients have increased susceptibility to graft versus host disease (GvHD) due to persistence of maternal lymphocytes, which enter the fetus via transplacental movement. GvHD may manifest as skin rashes, liver impairment, diarrhea, and blood cell abnormalities.

Early identification of SCID patients by newborn screening for T-cell receptor excision circles (TREC quantification test) has led to earlier treatment and increased survival of affected infants with overall cost savings. B
The TREC quantification test is currently used in all 50 states (90% of newborns in the USA) to screen for SCID. C

Suspect severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) in infants with a positive family history and those with persistent or recurrent oral thrush, recurrent pneumonia, intractable diarrhea, and rashes before 6 months of age, and infants who fail to thrive. C
Initial diagnostic tests should include a complete blood count, lymphocyte subset immunophenotyping, serum antibody levels, and in vitro lymphocyte proliferation tests. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Positive HIV DNA/RNA polymerase chain reaction; evidence of maternal HIV infection
Phenotypic spectrum-typical facial features, cardiac defects, neonatal tetany, cleft palate
Decreased expression of CD40 ligand on CD4 T cells; normal numbers of T and B cells on flow cytometry
Decreased immunoglobulins and low B-cell numbers on flow cytometry with normal levels of mature T cells

list.listitem: The definitive diagnosis of typical SCID requires that patients less than 2 years of age have: a) evidence of transplacental engraftment of maternal T cells; OR b) low numbers of T cells (CD3 T cells less than 300/μL), AND no or very low T-cell function lymphocyte (less than 10% lower limit of the normal range) as measured by response to mitogens such as phytohemagglutinin (PHA), and identification of mutation in a known SCID gene.

Diagnosis of leaky SCID requires reduced number of CD3 T cells (up to age 2 years, <1000/μL; for >2 to <4 years, <800/μL; for >4 years, 600/μL), reduced lymphocyte responses to PHA (<30% of normal T-cell function), absence of maternal T-cell engraftment, and presence of hypomorphic mutation in a known SCID gene.

Suspect severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) in infants with a positive family history and those with persistent or recurrent oral thrush, recurrent pneumonia, intractable diarrhea or other gastrointestinal symptoms, and rashes before 6 months of age, and infants who fail to thrive.

A family history of prior affected family member and /or parental consanguinity may be present. In a study of 50 patients with confirmed SCID, 27% of patients with typical SCID were diagnosed due to a positive family history, and these patients were diagnosed early (median age at diagnosis, 14 days, range 0-80 days).
Most SCID infants look normal at birth, but develop persistent or recurrent oral thrush, pneumonia, intractable diarrhea, and rashes before 6 months of age.

Recurrent infections lead to failure to thrive with poor gain of weight and length. The infections seen among 50 children with SCID were caused by Pneumocystis jirovecii (25%), viruses (25%; respiratory syncytial virus, rotavirus, enterovirus), candida (16%), and bacteria (16%). Some patients presented with simultaneous infections with more than one organism.

The TREC quantification test is currently used in 53 newborn screening programs in the USA and associated territories (90% of newborns in the USA) to screen for SCID. Test sensitivity, specificity, and PPV were 100%, 99.98%, and 45.8%, respectively.
If clinically suspected, initial diagnostic tests should include a complete blood count, lymphocyte phenotyping, serum antibody levels, and in vitro lymphocyte proliferation tests.

The complete blood count and differential are performed to check for the age-related absolute lymphocyte count. Mature T cells (CD3 T cells) account for approximately 70% of blood lymphocytes, so low lymphocyte counts generally indicate T-cell deficient conditions. Infants with absolute lymphocyte counts of less than 3000/mm3 should be evaluated for immune deficiency.
Tests for serum IgG, IgA, IgM (+/- IgE) are readily available and the presence of low IgG levels indicates the need for administration of IVIg to provide protection.

Lymphocyte immunophenotyping determines the levels of specific T-cell subsets, B cells, and NK cells, and shows the pattern of missing cells, which helps to delineate the likely form of SCID in different patients. The ratio of memory T cells to naïve T cells (CD45RO+/CD45RA+) determines the presence of maternal T cells, which typically have a memory phenotype (CD45RO+) compared with the naïve phenotype (CD45RA+) in infants. The presence of an abnormal lymphocyte subset analysis should trigger referral of the patient to an immunologist.

Measurement of lymphocyte proliferation is indicated if screening tests such as absolute lymphocyte count, lymphocyte immunophenotyping, and serum immunoglobulin are decreased. Proliferation rates of less than 10% lower limit of the normal range to mitogens such as PHA indicate a significant functional T-cell defect, as in SCID.
There may be a lack of thymic shadow on chest X-ray.
Consider HIV DNA/RNA polymerase chain reaction to rule out HIV infection if indicated.

Genetic testing for mutations of SCID genes is part of the advanced testing of a patient with suspected SCID and should ideally be performed by a clinical genetic service with expertise in immunodeficiency. In one study, 92% of patients with clinical SCID phenotype had mutations in genes associated with SCID.
SCID patients are best managed in dedicated pediatric units. C

Hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation with matched related and unrelated donor cells before the age of 3.5 months in an infection-free patient gives an overall 1-year survival of 86% (95% CI, 72% – 94%). B
Pegylated adenosine deaminase is used as replacement therapy in SCID due to adenosine deaminase deficiency, prior to definitive therapy as human stem-cell transplantation (HSCT).

SCID patients are best managed in dedicated pediatric units, with a mixture of conservative management (eg prophylactic antibiotics, immunoglobulin supplementation) and curative treatment (eg human stem-cell transplantation [HSCT], or gene-corrected autologous stem-cell transplants.

Hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation with matched related and unrelated donor cells before the age of 3.5 months in an infection-free patient gives an overall 1-year survival of 86% (95% CI, 72% – 94%). Gene therapy has also been used successfully to treat some forms of SCID.
Patients with suspected SCID should not receive live vaccines and the use of live vaccines in patients or household contacts should be suspended.

Patients with suspected SCID should receive prophylaxis against Pneumocystis jirovecii and pneumonia, and intravenous immunoglobulin-replacement therapy as prophylaxis against or management of other infections in the pre-transplantation period.
If indicated, only transfuse with CMV-negative, leukocyte-depleted, irradiated, packed red cells.
See Table 1 for a list of resources for physicians and patients.

Once the diagnosis is suspected from screening, a prior family history, or clinical suspicion, the patient should be referred immediately to a dedicated pediatric unit for further evaluation and management.
Optimal survival with full T-cell and antibody recovery following hematopoietic cell transplantation was most likely in patients who received grafts from matched sibling donors. B

Regardless of the donor, 5-year survival rates were high in patients who received transplantations at or before 3.5 months of age (94%), in older infants without prior infection (90%), and infants with resolved prior infection (82%).B

Patients are best followed up in specialist centers with tests for immune reconstitution and monitoring for long-term non-immune effects such as delayed growth, dental problems, hypothyroidism, neurocognitive defects, hearing impairment, and infertility. C
